lessons.tryIt: If you bake soon, try the windowpane test on your dough.

lessons.title: Lichen is a partnership
lessons.body: A lichen is not a single organism but a partnership between a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium. The fungus gives structure and shelter, while its partner makes food by photosynthesis. Many lichens are sensitive to air pollution, so their variety can hint at air quality.
lessons.tryIt: Look closely at a wall, tree or stone for crusty or leafy lichens.

lessons.title: Babies have more bones than adults
lessons.body: Newborns have around 300 bones and cartilage pieces, but adults have 206. Many bones fuse together as we grow, including those in the skull and at the base of the spine. The soft gaps in a baby's skull let it pass through the birth canal.
lessons.tryIt: Feel the bones in your wrist and remember several of them started out separate.

lessons.title: The planned cities of the Indus
lessons.body: Around 2500 BC, cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa had streets laid out in grids, standardised baked bricks and covered drains. Many houses had their own washing areas. Their script has still not been deciphered.
lessons.tryIt: Look at the drains on your street and think about how old the idea is.

lessons.title: The k in knight used to be spoken
lessons.body: Silent letters often reveal old pronunciations. In Old and Middle English, the k in 'knight' and 'knee' was pronounced, and the gh in 'night' was a throaty sound like in Scottish 'loch'. Spelling froze before the pronunciation changed.
lessons.tryIt: Say 'knight' with a pronounced k and a throaty gh, as it once sounded.

lessons.title: Let the silence sit
lessons.body: After asking a question, many people rush to fill a pause with another question or their own answer. Waiting a few seconds gives the other person time to think and often draws out a fuller, more honest reply. Teachers call this wait time.
lessons.tryIt: After your next question, count to three silently before saying anything.

lessons.title: Urgent is not the same as important
lessons.body: The Eisenhower matrix sorts tasks by whether they are urgent and whether they are important. Important but not urgent tasks, such as health, learning and relationships, are often neglected because nothing forces them. Scheduling them protects what matters.
lessons.tryIt: Write one important but not urgent task and give it a time slot this week.

lessons.title: Three kinds of lever
lessons.body: A lever has a pivot, an effort and a load. In a seesaw the pivot is in the middle; in a wheelbarrow the load sits between pivot and effort; in tweezers the effort is in the middle. Your forearm works like the third type, trading force for speed and range.
lessons.tryIt: Find one of each type of lever in your kitchen.

lessons.title: Thumbnails before the real drawing
lessons.body: Thumbnails are tiny, rough sketches, often just a few centimetres wide, used to test layouts before committing. Because they take seconds, you can try many arrangements and pick the strongest. Most composition problems are easier to spot small than large.
lessons.tryIt: Draw six stamp-sized thumbnails of the view from your window.

lessons.title: Reflections double the scene
lessons.body: Puddles, shop windows and still water can mirror a scene and create symmetry. Getting your lens very close to the surface of a puddle makes a tiny puddle look like a lake. Reflections are often most striking right after rain.
lessons.tryIt: Hold your phone just above a puddle or a glossy surface and look for a reflection.

lessons.title: The twelve-bar blues
lessons.body: The classic blues uses three chords over twelve bars: four bars of I, two of IV, two of I, then one each of V, IV, I and I. That frame supports countless songs, from early blues to rock and roll. Knowing it lets you predict where a song is going.
lessons.tryIt: Listen to a classic blues or rock and roll track and count the twelve bars.

lessons.title: The inverted pyramid
lessons.body: News stories traditionally put the most important facts first and the least important last. The first sentence answers who, what, when, where and why. Readers who stop early still get the essentials, which is a useful habit for emails too.
lessons.tryIt: Rewrite the first line of your next email so it states the main point.

lessons.title: Toast your nuts and seeds
lessons.body: Heating nuts and seeds in a dry pan for a few minutes deepens their flavour through browning and releases aromatic oils. Shake the pan often and remove them as soon as they smell nutty, since they can burn within seconds.
lessons.tryIt: Toast a handful of seeds or nuts in a dry pan and sprinkle them on a meal.

lessons.title: The dawn chorus
lessons.body: Birdsong is often loudest around dawn, especially in spring. Many songbirds sing to defend territory and attract mates, and the still, cool morning air helps sound carry. Different species tend to start at slightly different times.
lessons.tryIt: Open a window early tomorrow and listen for which birds start first.

lessons.title: Half-life
lessons.body: A radioactive isotope's half-life is the time it takes for half of its atoms to decay. After two half-lives, a quarter remain, then an eighth, and so on. Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years, which makes it useful for dating once-living material.
lessons.tryIt: Fold a sheet of paper in half repeatedly and see how quickly it gets tiny.

lessons.title: Fibonacci brought our numbers to Europe
lessons.body: In 1202, Leonardo of Pisa, later known as Fibonacci, published Liber Abaci. It introduced Europeans to the Hindu-Arabic numerals and showed how much easier they made trade calculations than Roman numerals. The famous Fibonacci sequence appears in it as a puzzle about rabbits.
lessons.tryIt: Try multiplying 23 by 14 in Roman numerals, then in normal digits.

lessons.title: Goodbye is a blessing
lessons.body: 'Goodbye' is a contraction of 'God be with ye', used in the sixteenth century. Over time it was shortened and the 'God' shifted to 'good', probably influenced by greetings like 'good day' and 'good night'. Many farewells hide old blessings.
lessons.tryIt: Notice how many ways you say goodbye today and what each one really means.

lessons.title: Use I statements
lessons.body: 'You never listen' sounds like an accusation and usually triggers defence. 'I feel unheard when I'm interrupted' describes your experience and invites the other person in. The facts may be the same, but the conversation goes very differently.
lessons.tryIt: Rephrase one complaint you have as an I statement.

lessons.title: Design your surroundings
lessons.body: Habits are shaped by friction. Putting a book on your pillow or a water bottle on your desk makes the good choice easy, while moving distracting apps off your home screen makes the bad one harder. Changing the environment often beats relying on willpower.
lessons.tryIt: Move one thing in your home to make a good habit easier.

lessons.title: The giant ball inside Taipei 101
lessons.body: Tall buildings sway in strong wind. Taipei 101 has a steel ball weighing around 660 tonnes hanging near its top as a tuned mass damper. When the building moves one way, the pendulum lags behind, absorbing energy and reducing the sway felt by people inside.
lessons.tryIt: Swing a bag on a string and feel it tug against your hand's motion.

lessons.title: The grid method
lessons.body: To copy an image accurately, draw a grid over a reference and a matching grid on your paper, then copy one square at a time. It breaks a hard drawing into small, simple shapes. Artists have used variations of this method for centuries to scale up images.
lessons.tryIt: Copy a small photo using a four-by-four grid.

lessons.title: White balance and colour temperature
lessons.body: Different light sources have different colours, measured in kelvin. Candlelight is very warm, around 1,900 K, midday sun is roughly 5,500 K, and open shade looks bluish. Cameras adjust white balance to make white look white, which is why indoor photos sometimes look orange.
lessons.tryIt: Photograph the same white paper under a lamp and by a window and compare.

lessons.title: Swing feel
lessons.body: In swing, pairs of equal notes are played long-short instead of evenly, giving a lilting bounce. It is notated the same way as straight rhythm, so it is a style rather than a different set of notes. Say 'humpty dumpty' with a bounce and you are close.
lessons.tryIt: Walk across a room in a long-short, long-short swing rhythm.

lessons.title: Write with smell
lessons.body: Writers lean heavily on sight and often forget the other senses. Smell is closely tied to memory and emotion, so a single scent can transport a reader. Wet pavement, burnt toast or new books can set a scene faster than a paragraph of description.
lessons.tryIt: Describe the room you are in using only what you can smell and hear.

lessons.title: Taste as you go
lessons.body: Seasoning a dish only at the end often leaves it uneven. Cooks taste at each stage, adding small amounts of salt or acid and adjusting before it is too late. Seasoning in layers builds flavour throughout instead of just on the surface.
lessons.tryIt: Taste your next dish three times while cooking and adjust each time.

lessons.title: Why owls fly silently
lessons.body: Many owls fly almost silently thanks to their feathers. Comb-like serrations on the leading edge of the wing, a fringe on the trailing edge and a soft, velvety surface all reduce turbulence and noise. Engineers have studied them to design quieter fans and blades.
lessons.tryIt: Wave a sheet of card through the air and notice how much noise it makes.

lessons.title: Why a straw works
lessons.body: When you suck on a straw, you lower the air pressure inside it. The atmosphere then pushes down on the surface of the drink and forces liquid up the straw. In theory, even perfect suction could lift water only about ten metres.
lessons.tryIt: Put your finger over the top of a straw in water and lift it out; watch the water stay.

lessons.title: Mondegreens
lessons.body: A mondegreen is a misheard lyric or phrase. The writer Sylvia Wright coined the word in 1954, after realising that a line of a Scottish ballad she had heard as 'Lady Mondegreen' was actually 'laid him on the green'. Everyone has a few.
lessons.tryIt: Think of a song lyric you misheard for years and say both versions aloud.

lessons.title: The liking gap
lessons.body: Research by Erica Boothby and colleagues in 2018 found that after conversations with strangers, people consistently underestimated how much their partner liked them. We are often harsher judges of our own social performance than others are.
lessons.tryIt: After your next chat, assume the other person enjoyed it more than you think.

lessons.title: The cost of switching
lessons.body: Switching between tasks carries a cost: each switch needs time to reorient, and errors increase. Research on task switching shows that even small switches add up. Batching similar tasks, such as replying to messages at set times, protects deep focus.
lessons.tryIt: Batch your messages into two set times today instead of checking constantly.

lessons.title: Why eight bits make 256
lessons.body: Each bit is either 0 or 1, so every extra bit doubles the number of possible combinations. Eight bits, called a byte, give 2 to the power 8, or 256 values. That is why many colour channels and old game limits stop at 255, since counting starts at zero.
lessons.tryIt: Count to ten in binary on your fingers, with each finger worth double the last.

lessons.title: Overlap for instant depth
lessons.body: When one shape partly covers another, we read the covered one as further away. Overlapping is one of the simplest depth cues and works even without shading or perspective. A row of shapes that only touch at the edges looks flat by comparison.
lessons.tryIt: Draw five pebbles or fruits so that each overlaps another.

lessons.title: The drone
lessons.body: A drone is a note or chord held continuously under a melody. In Indian classical music, the tanpura provides a constant drone that sets the tonal centre for the raga. Bagpipes use drones too. Against a steady drone, every melody note has a clear mood.
lessons.tryIt: Hum a steady low note and imagine a melody floating above it.

lessons.title: The iceberg theory
lessons.body: Ernest Hemingway argued that a writer can leave things out of a story if they know them well, and the reader will still feel them. Like an iceberg, only a small part shows above the surface. Unspoken subtext often carries more power than explanation.
lessons.tryIt: Write a two-line exchange where the characters avoid saying what they really mean.

lessons.title: Why milk cools chilli heat
lessons.body: Capsaicin, the compound behind chilli heat, activates the same nerve receptor that detects painful heat, which is why it feels hot. Capsaicin dissolves poorly in water, so water just spreads it around. Milk, yoghurt and other dairy foods tend to soothe the burn better.
lessons.tryIt: Keep some yoghurt on the table next time you eat something spicy.

lessons.title: Hot air rises
lessons.body: When air is heated, its molecules move faster and spread out, making it less dense than the cooler air around it. The cooler, denser air sinks and pushes the warm air up. This circulation, called convection, drives everything from radiator heating to thunderstorms.
lessons.tryIt: Hold your hand above and then beside a hot mug and feel the difference.

lessons.title: Woof is not universal
lessons.body: Onomatopoeia imitates sounds, but each language hears them differently. A dog says 'woof' in English, 'wan wan' in Japanese and 'guau' in Spanish. A rooster's call is 'cock-a-doodle-doo' in English but 'kikeriki' in German.
lessons.tryIt: Ask yourself how you would spell the sound your kettle or fridge makes.

lessons.title: Talk to strangers on the train
lessons.body: In studies by Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder, commuters asked to chat with a stranger reported a more pleasant journey than those who sat in silence, even though most predicted the opposite. Others were also more willing to talk than people expected.
lessons.tryIt: Exchange a few friendly words with someone you would normally ignore.

lessons.title: The Luhn check on your card
lessons.body: Most payment card numbers end with a check digit calculated by the Luhn formula, devised by Hans Peter Luhn at IBM. Doubling every second digit from the right and summing everything gives a multiple of ten. It catches any single mistyped digit and most swapped neighbours.
lessons.tryIt: Think about how a website can tell you mistyped a card number instantly.

lessons.title: Draw through the object
lessons.body: Construction drawing means sketching an object's simple underlying forms, including the hidden back edges, as if it were transparent. Boxes, cylinders and spheres become a scaffold for detail. It keeps proportions and perspective consistent before you commit to outlines.
lessons.tryIt: Draw a kettle as a cylinder and a box first, including the hidden lines.

lessons.title: Baking soda or baking powder
lessons.body: Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate, and it needs an acid such as buttermilk, yoghurt or lemon to release carbon dioxide. Baking powder already contains both the soda and a dry acid, so it only needs moisture and heat. They are not directly interchangeable.
lessons.tryIt: Check a favourite recipe to see which one it uses and why.

lessons.title: Sound can't cross space
lessons.body: Sound is a vibration passed from molecule to molecule, so it needs a medium like air, water or rock. In the near-vacuum of space there is almost nothing to carry it. Real explosions in space would be silent, whatever films suggest.
lessons.tryIt: Press your ear to a table while tapping it gently and hear sound travel through wood.

lessons.title: Why touchscreens ignore gloves
lessons.body: Most phone screens are capacitive: they hold a tiny electric field, and your conductive fingertip changes it at the point you touch. Ordinary gloves insulate your finger, so the screen cannot sense it. Touchscreen gloves have conductive threads in the fingertips.
lessons.tryIt: Try tapping your screen with a fingernail, a knuckle and a pen cap.

lessons.title: Crumple zones
lessons.body: A car's front and rear are designed to crumple in a crash. By crushing gradually, they extend the time it takes the car to stop, which reduces the force on the people inside. The strong passenger cell is designed not to deform.
lessons.tryIt: Drop an egg onto a folded towel and think about the extra stopping time.

lessons.title: Why manhole covers are round
lessons.body: A round cover cannot fall through its own hole, whichever way it is turned, because its width is the same in every direction. A square cover could drop through diagonally. Round covers can also be rolled and need no lining up before being dropped into place.
lessons.tryIt: Look at covers in your street and check which shapes have lips or frames.

lessons.title: How LEDs choose their colour
lessons.body: An LED glows when electrons drop across a gap in energy within a semiconductor and release light. The size of that band gap sets the colour. Most white LEDs are actually blue LEDs coated with a yellowish phosphor, which mix to look white.
lessons.tryIt: Look closely at a white LED bulb that is off and spot its yellow coating.
